Minimal Braces

This research is supported by Fundect-MS, CNPq and FAPESP (2018/04679-1) of Brazil, and by the Austrian Science Foundation FWF (START grant Y463).
Phelipe A. Fabres Affiliation: FACOM — UFMS, Campo Grande, Brasil    Nishad Kothari Affiliation: IC — UNICAMP, Campinas, Brasil    Marcelo H. de Carvalho Affiliation: FACOM — UFMS, Campo Grande, Brasil
1 September, 2020
Abstract

McCuaig (2001, Brace Generation, J. Graph Theory 38: 124-169) proved a generation theorem for braces, and used it as the principal induction tool to obtain a structural characterization of Pfaffian braces (2004, Pólya’s Permanent Problem, Electronic J. Combinatorics 11: R79).

A brace is minimal if deleting any edge results in a graph that is not a brace. From McCuaig’s brace generation theorem, we derive our main theorem that may be viewed as an induction tool for minimal braces. As an application, we prove that a minimal brace of order 2​n2n has size at most 5​n−105n-10, when n≥6n\geq 6, and we provide a complete characterization of minimal braces that meet this upper bound.

A similar work has already been done in the context of minimal bricks by Norine and Thomas (2006, Minimal Bricks, J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 96: 505-513) wherein they deduce the main result from the brick generation theorem due to the same authors (2007, Generating Bricks, J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 97: 769-817).

In memory of Robin Thomas

1 Bipartite matching covered graphs

For general graph-theoretic notation and terminology, we refer the reader to Bondy and Murty [1]. All graphs considered in this paper are finite and loopless; however, we do allow multiple (i.e., parallel) edges. For a graph GG, its order is the number of vertices (i.e., |V⁡(G)||V(G)|), and its size is the number of edges (i.e., |E⁡(G)||E(G)|). For a subset XX of V⁡(G)V(G), we denote by ∂(X)\partial(X) the cut associated with XX, and we refer to XX and X¯:=V⁡(G)−X\overline{X}:=V(G)-X as the shores of ∂(X)\partial(X). Thus ∂(X)\partial(X) is the set of edges that have exactly one end in either shore. A cut is trivial if either of its shores is a singleton. The graph obtained by contracting the shore XX to a single vertex xx is denoted by G/(X→x)G/(X\rightarrow x), or simply by G/XG/X. The two graphs G/XG/X and G/X¯G/\overline{X} are called the ∂(X)\partial(X)-contractions of GG.

A connected graph GG is kk-extendable if it has a matching of cardinality kk, and if each such matching extends to (i.e., is a subset of) a perfect matching of GG. For a comprehensive treatment of matching theory and its origins, we refer the reader to Lovász and Plummer [6]. All graphs considered in this paper are 11-extendable, and we shall instead refer to them as matching covered graphs. It is easily seen that these graphs (of order four or more) are 22-connected. Also, for a graph GG, we let nG:=|V⁡(G)|2n_{G}:=\frac{|V(G)|}{2} and mG:=|E⁡(G)|m_{G}:=|E(G)|; whence GG has order 2⋅nG2\cdot n_{G} and size mGm_{G}.

A cut ∂(X)\partial(X) of GG is tight if |M∩∂(X)|=1|M\cap\partial(X)|=1 for each perfect matching MM of GG. A matching covered graph that is free of nontrivial tight cuts is called a brace if it is bipartite, or otherwise a brick. It is easily verified that if ∂(X)\partial(X) is a nontrivial tight cut of a matching covered graph GG then each ∂(X)\partial(X)-contraction of GG is a matching covered graph of strictly smaller order. This observation leads to a decomposition of any matching covered graph into a list of bricks and braces; this procedure is known as a tight cut decomposition of GG. Clearly, a graph may admit several tight cut decompositions. However, Lovász [5] proved the remarkable result that any two tight cut decompositions of a matching covered graph GG yield the same list of bricks and braces (except possibly for the multiplicities of edges). We remark that GG is bipartite if and only if its tight cut decomposition yields only braces (i.e., it yields no bricks). The bipartite matching covered graph Q10Q_{10}, shown in Figure 1(a), has a nontrivial tight cut ∂(X)\partial(X), and each of its ∂(X)\partial(X)-contractions is isomorphic to the brace K3,3K_{3,3}.

Several important properties of a matching covered graph GG may be deduced by analysing its bricks and braces. (For instance, GG is Pfaffian if and only if each of its bricks and braces is Pfaffian; see [13, 4].) Consequently, researchers were led to gain a deeper understanding of bricks and braces. McCuaig [7] established a generation theorem for simple braces, and used this as the principal induction tool to obtain a structural characterization of Pfaffian braces [8]. Robertson, Seymour and Thomas [12] arrived at the same characterization using a different approach. (These groundbreaking works led to a polynomial-time algorithm for deciding whether or not a given bipartite graph is Pfaffian; see [9].)

A brace is minimal if deleting any edge results in a graph that is not a brace. The aforementioned McCuaig’s Theorem is a powerful induction tool for the class of simple braces. The object of this paper is to use McCuaig’s Theorem to derive an induction tool for the class of minimal braces — a proper subset of the class of simple braces. In the following three subsections, we introduce the necessary terminology to make this more precise.

A similar work has already been done in the context of minimal bricks by Norine and Thomas [10], wherein they deduce the main result from the brick generation theorem due to the same authors [11].

1.1 Braces

For a connected bipartite graph GG, we adopt the notation G⁡[A,B]G[A,B] to denote its color classes. We will generally use letters AA and BB to denote the color classes; sometimes we may instead use A′A^{\prime} and B′B^{\prime}. As shown in Figure 3, members of AA (or of A′A^{\prime}) will be denoted using letters aa and ww (with subscripts and/or superscripts) and will be depicted using hollow nodes; likewise, members of BB (or of B′B^{\prime}) will be denoted using letters bb and uu (with subscripts and/or superscripts) and will be depicted using solid nodes.

The neighborhood of a set of vertices ZZ is denoted by NG​(Z)N_{G}(Z). The following may be deduced from the well-known Hall’s Theorem.

Proposition 1.1

For a connected bipartite graph G⁡[A,B]G[A,B], where |A|=|B||A|=|B|, the following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    GG is matching covered,

  2. (ii)

    |NG​(Z)|≥|Z|+1|N_{G}(Z)|\geq|Z|+1 for every nonempty proper subset ZZ of AA, and

  3. (iii)

    G−a−bG-a-b has a perfect matching for each pair of vertices a∈Aa\in A and b∈Bb\in B. □\Box

Suppose that XX is an odd subset of the vertex set of a connected bipartite graph G⁡[A,B]G[A,B]. Then one of the two sets A∩XA\cap X and B∩XB\cap X is larger than the other; the larger set, denoted X+X_{+}, is called the majority part of XX; the smaller set, denoted X−X_{-}, is called the minority part of XX. The following proposition provides a convenient way of visualizing tight cuts in bipartite graphs. It is easily proved. (See Figure 1(a) for an example.)

Proposition 1.2

A cut ∂(X)\partial(X) of a bipartite matching covered graph G⁡[A,B]G[A,B] is tight if and only if the following hold:

  1. (i)

    |X||X| is odd and |X+|=|X−|+1|X_{+}|=|X_{-}|+1; consequently |X¯+|=|X¯−|+1|\overline{X}_{+}|=|\overline{X}_{-}|+1; and

  2. (ii)

    there are no edges between X−X_{-} and X¯−\overline{X}_{-}. □\Box

Recall that a brace is a bipartite matching covered graph that is free of nontrivial tight cuts. The following characterization of braces may be deduced from Proposition 1.2.

Proposition 1.3

For a connected bipartite graph G⁡[A,B]G[A,B] of order six or more, where |A|=|B||A|=|B|, the following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    GG is a brace,

  2. (ii)

    |NG​(Z)|≥|Z|+2|N_{G}(Z)|\geq|Z|+2 for every nonempty subset ZZ of AA such that |Z|<|A|−1|Z|<|A|-1,

  3. (iii)

    G−a1−a2−b1−b2G-a_{1}-a_{2}-b_{1}-b_{2} has a perfect matching for any four distinct vertices a1,a2∈Aa_{1},a_{2}\in A and b1,b2∈Bb_{1},b_{2}\in B,

  4. (iv)

    GG is 22-extendable. □\Box

Thus braces (of order at least four) are precisely those bipartite graphs that are 22-extendable. The following immediate consequence of Propositions 1.1 and 1.3 is worth noting.

Corollary 1.4

Let GG denote a bipartite graph obtained from a graph HH by adding an edge. If HH is matching covered then so is GG. Furthermore, if HH is a brace then so is GG. □\Box

The braces K2K_{2} and C4C_{4} are the only simple bipartite matching covered graphs of order at most four. For a bipartite matching covered graph GG of order six or more, it is easy to show that if GG has a 22-vertex-cut then GG has a nontrivial tight cut. This implies the following.

Proposition 1.5

Every brace, of order six or more, is 33-connected. □\Box

A vertex is cubic if its degree equals three; it is noncubic if it has degree four or more. A graph is cubic if each of its vertices is cubic, and it is noncubic if it has a noncubic vertex.

McCuaig [7] described three infinite families of simple braces: prisms11 1 McCuaig [7] refers to ‘prisms’ as ‘ladders’., Möbius ladders and biwheels. A biwheel of order 2​n2n (where n≥4n\geq 4), denoted B2​nB_{2n}, is the simple bipartite graph obtained from the cycle graph C2​n−2C_{2n-2} by adding two nonadjacent vertices — each of which has degree exactly n−1n-1. Observe that B2​nB_{2n} has size 4​n−44n-4. The cube B8B_{8}, shown in Figure 3(a), is the smallest biwheel. Except for B8B_{8}, biwheels are noncubic; see Figure 2(b).

On the other hand, prisms and Möbius ladders are cubic; we refer the interested reader to [3, 7] for descriptions of these families. The cube B8B_{8} is the smallest prism. The smallest Möbius ladders are K3,3K_{3,3} and the brace M10M_{10} shown in Figure 2(a). A McCuaig brace is any brace that is either a prism, or a Möbius ladder, or a biwheel.

1.2 McCuaig’s Theorem

An edge ee of a matching covered graph GG is removable if G−eG-e is also matching covered. The following is easily deduced from Propositions 1.1 and 1.3.

Corollary 1.6

In a brace, of order six or more, every edge is removable. □\Box

Now let GG denote a brace of order six or more, and let e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G). The bipartite matching covered graph G−eG-e may not be a brace. In particular, one or both ends of ee may have degree precisely two (in G−eG-e); in order to recover a smaller brace, at the very least, we must get rid of vertices of degree two. This brings us to the following notions of ‘bicontraction’ and ‘retract’.

Let GG be a matching covered graph, and let v0v_{0} denote a vertex of degree two that has two distinct neighbors, say v1v_{1} and v2v_{2}. The bicontraction of v0v_{0} is the operation of contracting the two edges v0​v1v_{0}v_{1} and v0​v2v_{0}v_{2} incident with v0v_{0}. Note that ∂(X)\partial(X), where X:={v0,v1,v2}X:=\{v_{0},v_{1},v_{2}\}, is a tight cut of GG. The graph obtained by bicontracting v0v_{0} is the same as G/XG/X and is thus matching covered. However, the bicontraction of a vertex of degree two in a simple graph need not result in a simple graph. The retract of GG, denoted G^\widehat{G}, is the matching covered graph obtained by bicontracting all its vertices of degree two that have two distinct neighbors.

For a brace GG of order six or more, a (removable) edge ee is thin if G−e^\widehat{G-e} is also a brace. Recently, Carvalho, Lucchesi and Murty [3] proved the following.

Theorem 1.7

Every brace, of order six or more, has at least two thin edges.

Note that if ee is a thin edge of a simple brace GG, the brace G−e^\widehat{G-e} may not be simple. A thin edge ee of a simple brace GG is strictly thin if the brace G−e^\widehat{G-e} is also simple. For instance, every edge of K3,3K_{3,3}, and of B8B_{8}, is thin but none of them is strictly thin. It is easily verified that every McCuaig brace has several thin edges; however, none of them is strictly thin. McCuaig showed that these are in fact the only simple braces with this property. We let 𝒢\mathcal{G} denote the set that comprises K2K_{2}, C4C_{4} and all McCuaig braces. McCuaig’s Theorem [7] may now be stated as follows.

Theorem 1.8

[McCuaig’s Theorem] Every simple brace G∉𝒢G\notin\mathcal{G} has a strictly thin edge.

Carvalho, Lucchesi and Murty gave an alternative proof of McCuaig’s Theorem using the existence of a thin edge; see [2]. In [3], the same authors establish a stronger version of McCuaig’s Theorem.

For a strictly thin edge ee of a simple brace GG, the index of ee, denoted index⁡(e){\rm index}(e), is the number of vertices of degree two in G−eG-e. Clearly, index⁡(e)∈{0,1,2}{\rm index}(e)\in\{0,1,2\}, depending on how many ends of ee are cubic in GG. The following is easily verified; see Figures 6 and 7.

Proposition 1.9

Let ee denote a strictly thin edge of a simple brace GG, and let H:=G−e^H:=\widehat{G-e}. Then nH=nG−index⁡(e)n_{H}=n_{G}-{\rm index}(e) and mH=mG−1−2⋅index⁡(e)m_{H}=m_{G}-1-2\cdot{\rm index}(e). □\Box

1.3 Minimal Braces

Recall that a brace GG is minimal if, for each e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G), the graph G−eG-e is not a brace. An edge ee of a simple brace GG is superfluous if G−eG-e is also a brace; note that a ‘superfluous edge’ is the same as a ‘strictly thin edge of index zero’. Thus, a minimal brace is a brace devoid of superfluous edges. Since any superfluous edge must join two noncubic vertices, the following holds.

Proposition 1.10

Let GG denote a brace of order six or more. If the set of all noncubic vertices is a stable set then GG is a minimal brace. □\Box

The graph B8+B_{8}^{+} shown in Figure 3(b), obtained from B8B_{8} by adding an edge, is the smallest simple brace that is not minimal; it has a unique superfluous edge. On the other hand, the graph Q10+Q_{10}^{+} shown in Figure 1(b), obtained from Q10Q_{10} by adding an edge, is minimal.

As stated earlier, our main objective is to derive an induction tool for the class of minimal braces from McCuaig’s Theorem.

Now let GG denote a minimal brace that is not a member of 𝒢\mathcal{G}. By McCuaig’s Theorem, GG has a strictly thin edge, say ee. We let HH denote the simple brace G−e^\widehat{G-e}. However, HH may not be a minimal brace. Clearly, we may choose a set F⊂E⁡(H)F\subset E(H) such that J:=H−FJ:=H-F is a minimal brace. (In this manner, we may recover a smaller minimal brace JJ.) Note that index⁡(e)∈{1,2}{\rm index}(e)\in\{1,2\}, each member of FF is a superfluous edge of HH, and that F=∅F=\emptyset if and only if HH is a minimal brace. This brings us to the following definition.

Definition 1.11

[Minimality-Preserving Pair] For a minimal brace GG, a pair (e,F)(e,F) is a minimality-preserving pair if ee is a strictly thin edge of GG, and FF is a subset of E⁡(G−e^)E(\widehat{G-e}) so that the graph G−e^−F\widehat{G-e}-F is a minimal brace.

In the above definition, since each edge of G−e^\widehat{G-e} naturally corresponds to an edge of GG, one may instead view the set FF as a subset of E⁡(G)E(G). Figure 3 shows an example of a minimal brace G:=Q10+G:=Q_{10}^{+} with a minimality-preserving pair (e,{f})(e,\{f\}) where index⁡(e)=1{\rm index}(e)=1.

The following is a trivial consequence of McCuaig’s Theorem.

Corollary 1.12

Every minimal brace G∉𝒢G\notin\mathcal{G} has a minimality-preserving pair (e,F)(e,F) for any strictly thin edge ee. □\Box

The next statement follows immediately from Proposition 1.9.

Proposition 1.13

Let (e,F)(e,F) denote a minimality-preserving pair of a minimal brace GG, and let J:=G−e^−FJ:=\widehat{G-e}-F. Then nJ=nG−index⁡(e)n_{J}=n_{G}-{\rm index}(e) and mJ=mG−1−2⋅index⁡(e)−|F|m_{J}=m_{G}-1-2\cdot{\rm index}(e)-|F|. □\Box

Corollary 1.12 may be viewed as an induction tool for minimal braces; however, it is not particularly useful for the following reason. If (e,F)(e,F) is a minimality-preserving pair of a minimal brace GG, then the minimal brace J:=G−e^−FJ:=\widehat{G-e}-F can be arbitrarily smaller in size than GG depending on the cardinality of the set FF. (This is in contrast to McCuaig’s Theorem; see Proposition 1.9). On the other hand, it seems intuitive that for a minimal brace G∉𝒢G\notin\mathcal{G} one should be able to find a minimality-preserving pair (e,F)(e,F) such that the set FF is “small”. This is in fact a consequence of our Main Theorem (3.12).

Corollary 1.14

Every minimal brace G∉𝒢G\notin\mathcal{G} has a minimality-preserving pair (e,F)(e,F) such that |F|≤index⁡(e)+1|F|\leq{\rm index}(e)+1.

Apart from this quantitative information regarding the minimality-preserving pair (e,F)(e,F), our Main Theorem (3.12) also provides qualitative information: for instance, each member of FF is at distance one from the strictly thin edge ee.

Organization of this paper: The Main Theorem (3.12) and its proof appear in Section 3. In Section 4, we use the Main Theorem as an induction tool to prove Theorem 4.2 — which states that mG≤5​nG−10m_{G}\leq 5n_{G}-10 for any minimal brace GG, where nG≥6n_{G}\geq 6, and also provides a complete characterization of minimal braces that meet this upper bound. In Section 2, we characterize minimal braces of small order; this will serve as the base case in our proof of Theorem 4.2.

2 Minimal braces of small order

Let ee denote any (removable) edge of a simple brace GG of order six or more. Note that ee is not superfluous if and only if the bipartite matching covered graph G−eG-e has a nontrivial tight cut. One may now easily deduce the following from Proposition 1.2.

Corollary 2.1

Let G⁡[A,B]G[A,B] denote a simple brace of order six or more. An edge ee of GG is not superfluous if and only if there exist partitions (A1,A2)(A_{1},A_{2}) of AA and (B1,B2)(B_{1},B_{2}) of BB such that |B1|=|A1|+1|B_{1}|=|A_{1}|+1 and ee is the only edge joining a vertex in A1A_{1} to a vertex in B2B_{2}. □\Box

The brace Q10+Q_{10}^{+}, shown in Figure 1(b), has precisely one edge joining two noncubic vertices, and it is not superfluous; consequently, Q10+Q_{10}^{+} is a minimal brace.

For a simple bipartite graph G⁡[A,B]G[A,B], its bipartite complement G¯\overline{G} is the graph that has the same set of vertices and has edge set {ab:ab∉E(G),a∈A,b∈B}\{ab:ab\notin E(G),a\in A,b\in B\}. Using this notion, one may easily prove that K3,3K_{3,3} and B8B_{8} are the only simple cubic bipartite graphs of order at most eight. (This proof technique is illustrated in the proof of Proposition 2.3.) Consequently, K3,3K_{3,3} is the only simple brace of order six. Using Corollary 2.1, one may infer that B8B_{8} is the only minimal brace of order eight.

Proposition 2.2

The only minimal braces of order at most eight are K2,C4,K3,3K_{2},C_{4},K_{3,3} and B8B_{8}. □\Box

Proposition 2.3

The only simple cubic bipartite graphs of order ten are M10M_{10} and Q10Q_{10}.

Proof: Let G⁡[A,B]G[A,B] denote a simple cubic bipartite graph of order ten, and let G¯\overline{G} denote its bipartite complement. Clearly, G¯\overline{G} is 22-regular. Observe the following. If G¯\overline{G} is disconnected then GG is isomorphic to Q10Q_{10}. Otherwise G¯\overline{G} is connected and GG is isomorphic to M10M_{10}. □\Box

Proposition 2.4

The only minimal braces of order ten are M10M_{10}, B10B_{10} and Q10+Q_{10}^{+}.

Proof: Let G⁡[A,B]G[A,B] denote a minimal brace of order ten. If GG is cubic then, by Proposition 2.3, GG is isomorphic to M10M_{10}. Now assume that GG is noncubic, and let TT denote the set of noncubic vertices.

First suppose that TT is a stable set. Observe that TT has precisely two members, say aa and bb, each of which has degree precisely four. Consequently, G−a−bG-a-b is a connected 22-regular bipartite graph. (Recall that braces of order six or more are 33-connected.) Thus G−a−bG-a-b is isomorphic to C8C_{8} and GG is isomorphic to B10B_{10}.

Now suppose that TT is not a stable set, and let e:=a​be:=ab denote an edge that joins a∈A∩Ta\in A\cap T and b∈B∩Tb\in B\cap T. Since GG is devoid of superfluous edges, the edge ee in particular is not superfluous. By Corollary 2.1, there exist partitions (A1,A2)(A_{1},A_{2}) of AA and (B1,B2)(B_{1},B_{2}) of BB such that |B1|=|A1|+1|B_{1}|=|A_{1}|+1 and ee is the only edge joining a vertex in A1A_{1} to a vertex in B2B_{2}. Since aa and bb are noncubic vertices, we infer that each of the sets B1B_{1} and A2A_{2} has at least three vertices. Consequently, |B1|=|A2|=3|B_{1}|=|A_{2}|=3, and each of the induced subgraphs G⁡[A1∪B1]G[A_{1}\cup B_{1}] and G⁡[A2∪B2]G[A_{2}\cup B_{2}] is isomorphic to K2,3K_{2,3}. Since |A1|=|B2|=2|A_{1}|=|B_{2}|=2, by Proposition 1.3, the induced subgraph G⁡[A2∪B1]G[A_{2}\cup B_{1}] has a perfect matching. All of these facts imply that the brace Q10+Q_{10}^{+} is a subgraph of GG, whence GG is isomorphic to Q10+Q_{10}^{+}. □\Box

Definition 2.5

[Stable-Extension] Let SS denote a stable set of a connected bipartite graph J⁡[A,B]J[A,B] that meets each color class in precisely two vertices. We let S:={a1,a2,b1,b2}S:=\{a_{1},a_{2},b_{1},b_{2}\} where a1,a2∈Aa_{1},a_{2}\in A and b1,b2∈Bb_{1},b_{2}\in B. The graph GG obtained from JJ — by adding two new vertices a0a_{0} and b0b_{0}, and five new edges a0​b1,a0​b2,b0​a1,b0​a2a_{0}b_{1},a_{0}b_{2},b_{0}a_{1},b_{0}a_{2} and a0​b0a_{0}b_{0} — is called the stable-extension of JJ with respect to SS — or simply the SS-extension of JJ. We refer to a0a_{0} and b0b_{0} as the extension vertices of GG.

The graph Q10Q_{10}, shown in Figure 4(a), has a unique stable set SS that meets each color class in precisely two vertices. We let Q12Q_{12}, shown in Figure 4(b), denote the SS-extension of Q10Q_{10}. Using Propositions 1.3 and 1.10, one may verify that Q12Q_{12} is a minimal brace.

Proposition 2.6

The only minimal braces of order 1212, and size at least 2020, are B12B_{12} and Q12Q_{12}.

Proof: Let G⁡[A,B]G[A,B] denote a minimal brace of order 1212 and size at least 2020, and let TT denote the set of noncubic vertices. Clearly, each of the sets T∩AT\cap A and T∩BT\cap B is nonempty. We let ETE_{T} denote the set of edges that have both ends in TT.

First suppose that TT is a stable set (i.e., ET=∅E_{T}=\emptyset), whence GG has maximum degree at most five. Observe that if there exists a vertex of degree five then |T∩A|=|T∩B|=1|T\cap A|=|T\cap B|=1; whence G−TG-T is a connected 22-regular bipartite graph; consequently, G−TG-T is isomorphic to C10C_{10} and GG is isomorphic to B12B_{12}. Otherwise, |T∩A|=|T∩B|=2|T\cap A|=|T\cap B|=2, and each member of TT has degree precisely four. In this case, observe that G−TG-T is a 11-regular (bipartite) graph; thus, G−TG-T has four components (each isomorphic to K2K_{2}), and GG is isomorphic to Q12Q_{12}.

Now suppose that TT is not a stable set. Our goal is to arrive at a contradiction; however, it requires some tedious arguments.

Let e:=a​be:=ab denote any member of ETE_{T}. Since ee is not superfluous, by Corollary 2.1, there exist partitions (A1,A2)(A_{1},A_{2}) of AA and (B1,B2)(B_{1},B_{2}) of BB such that |B1|=|A1|+1|B_{1}|=|A_{1}|+1 and ee is the only edge joining a vertex in A1A_{1} to a vertex in B2B_{2}. Since each end of ee is noncubic, and since nG=6n_{G}=6, one of the two sets B1B_{1} and A2A_{2} has cardinality three and the other one has cardinality four. Adjust notation so that |B1|=3|B_{1}|=3 and |A2|=4|A_{2}|=4. See Figure 5(a). Let a1a_{1} denote the unique member of A1−aA_{1}-a. Observe that NG​(a)=B1∪{b}N_{G}(a)=B_{1}\cup\{b\} and NG​(a1)=B1N_{G}(a_{1})=B_{1}.

In particular, we have proved the following.

2.6.1

Each edge f∈ETf\in E_{T} has an end whose degree is precisely four, say vv, such that there exists a cubic vertex v′v^{\prime} that satisfies NG​(v′)=NG−f​(v)N_{G}(v^{\prime})=N_{G-f}(v). □\Box

The degree of vertex bb is either four or five; we will prove that it must be four. Suppose to the contrary that bb has degree five; whence NG​(b):=A2∪{a}N_{G}(b):=A_{2}\cup\{a\}. By a simple counting argument, there exists a noncubic vertex, say a2a_{2}, in A2A_{2}. Since f2:=a2​bf_{2}:=a_{2}b is a member of ETE_{T}, using statement 2.6.1, we infer that a2a_{2} has degree precisely four, and there exists a cubic vertex a′a^{\prime} that satisfies NG​(a′)=NG−f2​(a2)=NG​(a2)−bN_{G}(a^{\prime})=N_{G-f_{2}}(a_{2})=N_{G}(a_{2})-b. Since each member of A2A_{2} is adjacent with bb, it follows that a′=a1a^{\prime}=a_{1}. Consequently, NG​(a2)=B1∪{b}N_{G}(a_{2})=B_{1}\cup\{b\}. This implies that NG​(B2−b)⊆A2−a2N_{G}(B_{2}-b)\subseteq A_{2}-a_{2}. This contradicts Proposition 1.3. Thus bb has degree four.

In particular, we have now proved the following.

2.6.2

For every edge f∈ETf\in E_{T}, each end of ff has degree precisely four. (Consequently, |T∩A|=|T∩B|≥2|T\cap A|=|T\cap B|\geq 2, and each vertex in TT has degree precisely four.) □\Box

Now, we will prove that each neighbor of aa, distinct from bb, is cubic. Suppose to the contrary that there exists b1∈B1b_{1}\in B_{1} that is noncubic. Thus b1b_{1} has degree precisely four and f1:=a​b1f_{1}:=ab_{1} is a member of ETE_{T}. Now we invoke statement 2.6.1. Either there exists a cubic vertex a′a^{\prime} that satisfies NG​(a′)=NG−f1​(a)=(B1−b1)∪{b}N_{G}(a^{\prime})=N_{G-f_{1}}(a)=(B_{1}-b_{1})\cup\{b\}, or otherwise there exists a cubic vertex b′b^{\prime} that satisfies NG​(b′)=NG−f1​(b1)=NG​(b1)−aN_{G}(b^{\prime})=N_{G-f_{1}}(b_{1})=N_{G}(b_{1})-a. In the latter case, note that b′∈B2b^{\prime}\in B_{2} (since each vertex in B1B_{1} is adjacent with aa); however, this implies that we have an edge joining b′∈B2b^{\prime}\in B_{2} and a1∈A1a_{1}\in A_{1}; contradiction. In the former case, note that a′∈A2a^{\prime}\in A_{2}; whence NG​(B2−b)⊆A2−a′N_{G}(B_{2}-b)\subseteq A_{2}-a^{\prime}, and this contradicts Proposition 1.3. Thus each neighbor of aa, distinct from bb, is cubic; see Figure 5(b).

In particular, we have established the following.

2.6.3

For every edge f∈ETf\in E_{T}, each end of ff has degree precisely four (in GG) and at least one of them has degree precisely one in the induced subgraph G⁡[T]G[T]. □\Box

We let w∈Aw\in A and u∈Bu\in B denote two vertices of TT that are distinct from aa and bb. Note that w∈A2w\in A_{2} and u∈B2u\in B_{2}. By Proposition 1.3, the graph G−a−a1−b−uG-a-a_{1}-b-u has a perfect matching; whence the three edges joining B1B_{1} and A2A_{2} constitute a matching. This implies that ww has precisely one neighbor in B1B_{1}. Consequently, w​b,w​u∈E⁡(G)wb,wu\in E(G). Observe that the induced subgraph G⁡[T]G[T] contains a path of length three: (a,b,w,u)(a,b,w,u). The edge b​w∈ETbw\in E_{T} contradicts statement 2.6.3.

This completes the proof of Proposition 2.6. □\Box

3 An induction tool for minimal braces

In subsection 1.2, we presented a ‘reduction version’ of McCuaig’s Theorem (1.8) using the notion of a strictly thin edge; this viewpoint and the associated terminology is due to Carvalho, Lucchesi and Murty [2, 3] and it is convenient for stating results concisely. In the following subsection, we shall present a ‘generation version’ of McCuaig’s Theorem (3.4). In order to do so, we first need to define some ‘expansion operations’; these will also be useful in deducing our Main Theorem (3.12).

3.1 Expansion operations

For a simple bipartite connected graph H⁡[A,B]H[A,B], and nonadjacent vertices a∈Aa\in A and b∈Bb\in B, H+a​bH+ab denotes the graph obtained from HH by adding the edge a​bab. Note that if HH is a brace then, by Corollary 1.4, H+a​bH+ab is a (simple) brace and a​bab is a strictly thin edge of index zero; in this case, we say that H+a​bH+ab is obtained from HH by an expansion of index zero. We shall now define two more expansion operations (on simple braces) — each of which may be viewed as the reverse of removing a strictly thin edge (of index one or two) and then taking the retract. To do so, we first need the notion of ‘bi-splitting’ a noncubic vertex.

Let bb denote a noncubic vertex of a simple bipartite matching covered graph H⁡[A′,B′]H[A^{\prime},B^{\prime}]. Adjust notation so that b∈B′b\in B^{\prime}. Suppose that a (bipartite) graph GG is obtained from HH by replacing the vertex bb by two new vertices b1b_{1} and b2b_{2}, distributing the edges in HH incident with bb between b1b_{1} and b2b_{2} such that each gets at least two edges, and then adding a new vertex a0a_{0} and two new edges: a0​b1,a0​b2a_{0}b_{1},a_{0}b_{2}. We say that GG is obtained from HH by bi-splitting bb into b1​a0​b2b_{1}a_{0}b_{2}, and we denote this as G:=H{b→b1a0b2}G:=H\{b\rightarrow b_{1}a_{0}b_{2}\}. It is easily verified that GG is also matching covered. Observe that HH can be recovered from GG by bicontracting the vertex a0a_{0} and denoting the contraction vertex by bb.

We are now ready to define the aforementioned expansion operations. (See Figures 6 and 7.)

Definition 3.1

[Expansion of Index One] Choose two vertices, say aa and ww, of a simple brace HH that belong to the same color class such that at least one of them, say aa, is noncubic. A graph GG is obtained from HH by an expansion of index one if G:=H{a→a1b0a2}+b0wG:=H\{a\rightarrow a_{1}b_{0}a_{2}\}+b_{0}w.

As an example, one may construct the brace Q12Q_{12} from the brace Q10+Q_{10}^{+} by means of an expansion of index zero (i.e., adding an edge) followed by an expansion of index one. To see this, we let Q10+:=Q10+a1​b1Q_{10}^{+}:=Q_{10}+a_{1}b_{1} as per the labeling in Figure 4(a). Now, observe that, as per the labeling in Figure 4(b), Q12:=(Q10++a1b2){a1→a1b0a0}+b0a2Q_{12}:=(Q_{10}^{+}+a_{1}b_{2})\{a_{1}\rightarrow a_{1}b_{0}a_{0}\}+b_{0}a_{2}.22 2 In order to be consistent with the labeling used in Figures 4(a) and 4(b), we slightly abuse notation by overloading the label a1a_{1}.

Definition 3.2

[Expansion of Index Two] Choose two noncubic vertices, say aa and bb, of a simple brace HH that lie in distinct color classes. A graph GG is obtained from HH by an expansion of index two if G:=H{a→a1b0a2}{b→b1a0b2}+a0b0G:=H\{a\rightarrow a_{1}b_{0}a_{2}\}\{b\rightarrow b_{1}a_{0}b_{2}\}+a_{0}b_{0}.

For convenience, we say that a graph GG is obtained from the simple brace HH by an expansion operation if GG is obtained from HH by an expansion of index zero, one or two. McCuaig [7] proved the following.

Proposition 3.3

Any graph GG, that is obtained from a simple brace HH by an expansion operation, is also a simple brace.

Let H⁡[A,B]H[A,B] denote a simple brace. Observe the following. If G:=H{a→a1b0a2}+b0wG:=H\{a\rightarrow a_{1}b_{0}a_{2}\}+b_{0}w for some a,w∈Aa,w\in A, then e:=b0​we:=b_{0}w is a strictly thin edge of index one. On the other hand, if G:=H{a→a1b0a2}{b→b1a0b2}+a0b0G:=H\{a\rightarrow a_{1}b_{0}a_{2}\}\{b\rightarrow b_{1}a_{0}b_{2}\}+a_{0}b_{0} for some a∈Aa\in A and b∈Bb\in B, then e:=a0​b0e:=a_{0}b_{0} is a strictly thin edge of index two. In either case, HH is isomorphic to G−e^\widehat{G-e}. We now state the ‘generation version’ of McCuaig’s Theorem (that is equivalent to Theorem 1.8.)

Theorem 3.4

Every simple brace G∉𝒢G\notin\mathcal{G} may be obtained from a (smaller) simple brace by an expansion operation.

In the following two subsections, we state and prove several lemmas; these will culminate in the proof of the Main Theorem (3.12) that appears in subsection 3.4. However, we need some more terminology in order to state these lemmas.

Consider the graph G−eG-e where ee is a strictly thin edge of a simple brace GG. In G−eG-e, a vertex of degree two is referred to as an inner vertex, and each of its neighbors is referred to as an outer vertex. Note that G−eG-e has precisely index⁡(e){\rm index}(e) inner vertices and 2⋅index⁡(e)2\cdot{\rm index}(e) outer vertices; see Figures 6 and 7.

3.2 Index one

Throughout this subsection, we assume that G⁡[A,B]∉𝒢G[A,B]\notin\mathcal{G} is a minimal brace, and that e:=b0​we:=b_{0}w is a strictly thin edge of index one where b0∈Bb_{0}\in B is the cubic end of ee. We also assume that the simple brace H:=G−e^H:=\widehat{G-e} is not minimal; whence HH has superfluous edge(s). Thus nH≥4n_{H}\geq 4 and nG≥5n_{G}\geq 5. We let a1a_{1} and a2a_{2} denote the outer vertices of G−eG-e. See Figure 6.

Lemma 3.5

Let ff denote any superfluous edge of HH. Then G−eG-e has a cubic outer vertex that is an end of ff, whereas the other end of ff is noncubic.

Proof: Recall definition 3.1, and observe the following. If each of a1a_{1} and a2a_{2} has degree at least three in G−fG-f, then G−fG-f may be obtained from the brace H−fH-f by an expansion of index one; whence G−fG-f is a brace (by Proposition 3.3); contradiction. It follows that one of a1a_{1} and a2a_{2} is a cubic end of ff. Clearly, the other end of ff is noncubic. □\Box

Lemma 3.6

Let f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} denote two edges of HH such that H−f1−f2H-f_{1}-f_{2} is a brace. Then G−eG-e has a cubic outer vertex that is a common end of f1f_{1} and f2f_{2}.

Proof: It follows from the hypothesis that each of f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} is a superfluous edge of HH. By Lemma 3.5, for i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}, the edge fif_{i} has precisely one cubic end (in GG) that lies in {a1,a2}\{a_{1},a_{2}\}. If the cubic end of f1f_{1} is the same as the cubic end of f2f_{2}, then there is nothing to prove.

Now suppose that fi∈∂(ai)f_{i}\in\partial(a_{i}) for i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}. Consequently, a1a_{1} and a2a_{2} are both cubic (in GG), whence aa has degree precisely four in HH; consequently, aa is a vertex of degree two in H−f1−f2H-f_{1}-f_{2}; contradiction. □\Box

Note that, if (e,F)(e,F) is a minimality-preserving pair of GG then any two distinct members of FF, say f1f_{1} and f2f_{2}, satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma 3.6. We thus have the following immediate consequence.

Corollary 3.7

If (e,F)(e,F) is a minimality-preserving pair of GG, then G−eG-e has a cubic outer vertex vv such that F⊂∂(v)F\subset\partial(v). Consequently, |F|∈{1,2}|F|\in\{1,2\}. □\Box

Lemma 3.8

Suppose that (e,F)(e,F) is a minimality-preserving pair of GG such that |F|=2|F|=2. Then, for each f∈Ff\in F, the noncubic end of ff is not adjacent with the noncubic end of ee. Moreover, GG is isomorphic to a stable-extension of the minimal brace J:=G−e^−FJ:=\widehat{G-e}-F.

Proof: Let F:={f1,f2}F:=\{f_{1},f_{2}\}. We invoke Lemma 3.6, and adjust notation so that a1a_{1} is cubic and f1,f2∈∂(a1)f_{1},f_{2}\in\partial(a_{1}). We let u1u_{1} and u2u_{2} denote the noncubic ends of f1f_{1} and f2f_{2}, respectively. We let J:=H−FJ:=H-F. Thus JJ is a minimal brace. See Figure 8.

Our goal is to prove that w​u1,w​u2∉E⁡(G)wu_{1},wu_{2}\notin E(G). By symmetry, it suffices to prove that w​u2∉E⁡(G)wu_{2}\notin E(G). Suppose to the contrary that w​u2∈E⁡(G)wu_{2}\in E(G). See Figure 9.

In this case, ww and u2u_{2} are adjacent in JJ as well. Observe that one may obtain the graph G′:=G−w​u2G^{\prime}:=G-wu_{2} from the brace J′:=J+a​u2J^{\prime}:=J+au_{2} by an expansion of index one. In particular, G′=J′{u2→u2a1b0}+a1u1G^{\prime}=J^{\prime}\{u_{2}\rightarrow u_{2}a_{1}b_{0}\}+a_{1}u_{1}. By Proposition 3.3, G′G^{\prime} is a brace — contrary to our hypothesis that GG is minimal.

We thus conclude that w​u1,w​u2∉E⁡(G)wu_{1},wu_{2}\notin E(G). Consequently, S:={a,w,u1,u2}S:=\{a,w,u_{1},u_{2}\} is a stable set of JJ that meets each color class in two vertices. Observe that GG is isomorphic to the SS-extension of JJ (with a1a_{1} and b0b_{0} playing the role of the extension vertices). This completes the proof of Lemma 3.8. □\Box

3.3 Index two

Throughout this subsection, we assume that G⁡[A,B]∉𝒢G[A,B]\notin\mathcal{G} is a minimal brace that is devoid of strictly thin edges of index one, and that e:=a0​b0e:=a_{0}b_{0} is a strictly thin edge of index two. We also assume that the simple brace H:=G−e^H:=\widehat{G-e} is not minimal; whence HH has superfluous edge(s). Thus nH≥4n_{H}\geq 4 and nG≥6n_{G}\geq 6. We let a1,a2∈Aa_{1},a_{2}\in A and b1,b2∈Bb_{1},b_{2}\in B denote the outer vertices of G−eG-e. See Figure 7.

Since ee is a strictly thin edge, GG has at most one edge that has one end in {a1,a2}\{a_{1},a_{2}\} and the other end in {b1,b2}\{b_{1},b_{2}\}; furthermore, GG has (precisely) one such edge if and only if a​b∈E⁡(H)ab\in E(H).

Lemma 3.9

Let ff denote any superfluous edge of HH. Then G−eG-e has a cubic outer vertex that is an end of ff; the other end of ff is either noncubic, or it is another cubic outer vertex.

Proof: Recall definition 3.2, and observe the following. If each of a1,a2,b1,b2a_{1},a_{2},b_{1},b_{2} has degree at least three in G−fG-f, then G−fG-f may be obtained from the brace H−fH-f by an expansion of index two; whence G−fG-f is a brace (by Proposition 3.3); contradiction. It follows that one of a1,a2,b1,b2a_{1},a_{2},b_{1},b_{2} is a cubic end of ff. Adjust notation so that a1a_{1} is a cubic end of ff. Clearly, if the other end of ff is not in {b1,b2}\{b_{1},b_{2}\} then it is noncubic.

Now suppose that the other end of ff is in {b1,b2}\{b_{1},b_{2}\}; adjust notation so that f:=a1​b1f:=a_{1}b_{1}. Assume that b1b_{1} is noncubic. Let uu denote the neighbor of a1a_{1} that is distinct from b0b_{0} and b1b_{1}. See Figure 10. Observe that the graph G−f^\widehat{G-f} may be obtained from the brace H−fH-f by an expansion of index one; in particular, G−f^:=(H−f){b→b1a0b2}+a0u\widehat{G-f}:=(H-f)\{b\rightarrow b_{1}a_{0}b_{2}\}+a_{0}u. Thus G−f^\widehat{G-f} is a brace (by Proposition 3.3). Consequently, ff is a strictly thin edge of index one, contrary to our hypothesis that GG is devoid of such edges. Thus b1b_{1} is also cubic. □\Box

Lemma 3.10

Let ff denote any superfluous edge of HH. Then, in G−eG-e, either ff joins two outer vertices, or otherwise ff is adjacent with an edge that joins two outer vertices.

Proof: By Lemma 3.9, G−eG-e has a cubic outer vertex that is an end of ff. Adjust notation so that a1a_{1} is a cubic end of ff. If the other end of ff lies in {b1,b2}\{b_{1},b_{2}\} then we are done.

Now suppose that f∉∂({b1,b2})f\notin\partial(\{b_{1},b_{2}\}), and let u′u^{\prime} denote the noncubic end of ff. Assume that a1​b1,a1​b2∉E⁡(G)a_{1}b_{1},a_{1}b_{2}\notin E(G). Let uu denote the neighbor of a1a_{1} that is distinct from b0b_{0} and u′u^{\prime}. Note that u∉{b1,b2}u\notin\{b_{1},b_{2}\}. See Figure 11. Observe that the graph G−f^\widehat{G-f} may be obtained from the brace H−fH-f by an expansion of index one; in particular, G−f^:=(H−f){b→b1a0b2}+a0u\widehat{G-f}:=(H-f)\{b\rightarrow b_{1}a_{0}b_{2}\}+a_{0}u. Thus G−f^\widehat{G-f} is a brace (by Proposition 3.3). Consequently, ff is a strictly thin edge of index one, contrary to our hypothesis that GG is devoid of such edges. Thus, one of a1​b1a_{1}b_{1} and a1​b2a_{1}b_{2} is an edge of GG; whence ff is adjacent with an edge that joins two outer vertices. □\Box

Corollary 3.11

If (e,F)(e,F) is a minimality-preserving pair of GG, then G−eG-e has two adjacent outer vertices uu and ww such that F⊂∂(u)∪∂(w)F\subset\partial(u)\cup\partial(w). Furthermore, if F∩∂(u)≠∅F\cap\partial(u)\neq\emptyset then uu is cubic; likewise, if F∩∂(w)≠∅F\cap\partial(w)\neq\emptyset then ww is cubic. Consequently, |F|∈{1,2,3}|F|\in\{1,2,3\}. □\Box

3.4 Main Theorem

We are now ready to state and prove the Main Theorem.

Theorem 3.12

[Main Theorem] Every minimal brace G∉𝒢G\notin\mathcal{G} has a minimality-preserving pair (e,F)(e,F) such that either F=∅F=\emptyset, or otherwise FF satisfies the following properties in G−eG-e:

  1. (i)

    If index⁡(e)=1{\rm index}(e)=1 then G−eG-e has an outer vertex, say vv, such that F⊂∂(v)F\subset\partial(v).

  2. (ii)

    If index⁡(e)=2{\rm index}(e)=2 then G−eG-e has two adjacent outer vertices, say uu and ww, such that F⊂∂(u)∪∂(w)F\subset\partial(u)\cup\partial(w).

  3. (iii)

    For each f∈Ff\in F, an end of ff is cubic if and only if it is an outer vertex.

Consequently, |F|≤index⁡(e)+1|F|\leq{\rm index}(e)+1. Furthermore, if index⁡(e)=1{\rm index}(e)=1 and |F|=2|F|=2 then GG is isomorphic to a stable-extension of the minimal brace J:=G−e^−FJ:=\widehat{G-e}-F.

Proof: By McCuaig’s Theorem and its corollary (1.12), GG has a strictly thin edge (of index one or two); furthermore, for any such edge ee, there exists a minimality-preserving pair (e,F)(e,F).

If GG has a strictly thin edge of index one, say ee, then we choose any minimality-preserving pair (e,F)(e,F), and we are done by invoking Lemma 3.5, Corollary 3.7 and Lemma 3.8.

Now suppose that GG is devoid of strictly thin edges of index one. Thus GG has a strictly thin edge of index two, say ee. We choose any minimality-preserving pair (e,F)(e,F), and we are done by invoking Lemma 3.9 and Corollary 3.11. □\Box

For convenience, let us introduce the following definition.

Definition 3.13

[Narrow Minimality-Preserving Pair] A minimality-preserving pair (e,F)(e,F) of a minimal brace GG is narrow if it satisfies the statement of the Main Theorem (3.12).

We may thus condense the statement of the Main Theorem as follows: every minimal brace G∉𝒢G\notin\mathcal{G} has a narrow minimality-preserving pair.

Recall that we presented two equivalent versions of McCuaig’s Theorem: first a ‘reduction version’ (1.8), and second a ‘generation version’ (3.4). In the same spirit, Theorem 3.12 (as stated) may be viewed as a ‘reduction version’ for minimal braces. The interested reader may obtain a ‘generation version’ (equivalent to Theorem 3.12) for minimal braces by defining ‘extension operations’ that could be potentially useful in obtaining a (larger) minimal brace from a (smaller) minimal brace. Each such extension operation may be viewed as a sequence of index zero expansions (possibly none) followed by an index one or index two expansion with some additional restrictions (depending on the cardinality and structure of the set FF and the index of the strictly thin edge ee). This is in fact the viewpoint adopted by Norine and Thomas [10] in their paper on minimal bricks.

We shall not define all of the aforementioned extension operations here (except for the one we have already described: Definition 2.5). The reader may verify that if a graph GG is isomorphic to a stable-extension of a simple brace JJ, then GG may be obtained from JJ by first adding two (adjacent) edges and then performing an index one expansion. This observation, coupled with Proposition 3.3, yields the following.

Corollary 3.14

Any graph GG, that is isomorphic to a stable-extension of a simple brace JJ, is also a simple brace. □\Box

4 An application

In this section, as an application of the Main Theorem (3.12), we will prove that if GG is a minimal brace (where nG≥6n_{G}\geq 6) then mG≤5⋅nG−10m_{G}\leq 5\cdot n_{G}-10; furthermore, we shall provide a complete characterization of minimal braces that meet this upper bound.

We begin by defining an infinite family 𝒬\mathcal{Q} of minimal braces, each of whose members meets this upper bound; its smallest member is Q12Q_{12}. For n≥7n\geq 7, we define the graph Q2​nQ_{2n} as the SS-extension of Q2​n−2Q_{2n-2} — where the set SS comprises the noncubic vertices of Q2​n−2Q_{2n-2}. Now let 𝒬:={Q2​n:n≥6}\mathcal{Q}:=\{Q_{2n}:n\geq 6\}. Since Q12Q_{12} is a simple brace, it follows from Corollary 3.14 that each member of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is a simple brace. Furthermore, by Proposition 1.10, we infer that each member of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is in fact a minimal brace. By summing degrees, observe that if G∈𝒬G\in\mathcal{Q} then mG=5⋅nG−10m_{G}=5\cdot n_{G}-10.

We now prove the following easy corollary of the Main Theorem.

Corollary 4.1

Let (e,F)(e,F) denote a narrow minimality-preserving pair of a minimal brace GG, and let J:=G−e^−FJ:=\widehat{G-e}-F. Assume that mJ≤5⋅nJ−10m_{J}\leq 5\cdot n_{J}-10. Then the following hold:

  1. (i)

    mG≤5⋅nG−10m_{G}\leq 5\cdot n_{G}-10.

  2. (ii)

    If mG=5⋅nG−10m_{G}=5\cdot n_{G}-10 then mJ=5⋅nJ−10m_{J}=5\cdot n_{J}-10, index⁡(e)=1{\rm index}(e)=1 and |F|=2|F|=2; consequently, GG is isomorphic to a stable-extension of JJ.

Proof: By Proposition 1.13, nJ=nG−index⁡(e)n_{J}=n_{G}-{\rm index}(e) and mG=mJ+1+2⋅index⁡(e)+|F|m_{G}=m_{J}+1+2\cdot{\rm index}(e)+|F|. By Theorem 3.12, |F|≤index⁡(e)+1|F|\leq{\rm index}(e)+1. We now consider two cases depending on the index of ee.

First consider the case: index⁡(e)=2{\rm index}(e)=2. Using the equations and inequalities noted above, we have: mG=mJ+5+|F|<(5⋅nJ−10)+5+5=5⋅nJ=5⋅nG−10.m_{G}=m_{J}+5+|F|<(5\cdot n_{J}-10)+5+5=5\cdot n_{J}=5\cdot n_{G}-10. Thus, in this case, the strict inequality mG<5⋅nG−10m_{G}<5\cdot n_{G}-10 holds.

Now consider the case: index⁡(e)=1{\rm index}(e)=1. Using the same equations and inequalities as before, we have: mG=mJ+3+|F|≤(5⋅nJ−10)+3+2=5⋅nJ−5=5⋅nG−10m_{G}=m_{J}+3+|F|\leq(5\cdot n_{J}-10)+3+2=5\cdot n_{J}-5=5\cdot n_{G}-10. Hence, we have the inequality mG≤5⋅nG−10m_{G}\leq 5\cdot n_{G}-10; equality holds if and only if mJ=5⋅nJ−10m_{J}=5\cdot n_{J}-10 and |F|=2|F|=2. By the last part of Theorem 3.12, we infer that GG is isomorphic to a stable-extension of JJ. This completes the proof of Corollary 4.1. □\Box

We are now ready to prove the main result of this section.

Theorem 4.2

Let GG denote a minimal brace that is not in {K2,C4,K3,3,B8,B10,Q10+}\{K_{2},C_{4},K_{3,3},B_{8},B_{10},Q_{10}^{+}\}. Then mG≤5⋅nG−10m_{G}\leq 5\cdot n_{G}-10, and equality holds if and only if G∈{M10,B12}∪𝒬G\in\{M_{10},B_{12}\}\cup\mathcal{Q}.

Proof: We proceed by induction on the order of the graph. Let G⁡[A,B]G[A,B] denote a minimal brace that is not in {K2,C4,K3,3,B8,B10,Q10+}\{K_{2},C_{4},K_{3,3},B_{8},B_{10},Q_{10}^{+}\}.

The reader may verify, using Propositions 2.2 and 2.4, that the desired conclusion holds when nG≤5n_{G}\leq 5. Now suppose that nG≥6n_{G}\geq 6. If GG is cubic then mG=3⋅nG<5⋅nG−10m_{G}=3\cdot n_{G}<5\cdot n_{G}-10. We may thus assume that GG is noncubic.
